comment: Example client configs for laptops on the same LAN. Replace 'your-mac.local' with your host's mDNS name or LAN IP. The domestic template serves SIX lanes from one endpoint: 'heavy' + 'medium' + 'flash' + 'super-flash' (cloud) and 'local-orch' + 'local-sub' (host GPU). A lane name is the stable contract - the host can swap the model behind it without any client edit. The cloud defaults pin build/plan to 'heavy', the custom 'standard' subagent to 'medium' when advertised (otherwise 'flash'), the custom 'light' subagent and explore to 'flash', and compaction/title/summary to 'super-flash'; the built-in 'general' agent is disabled. The global model and small_model are 'heavy' and 'super-flash'. `--small-model` explicitly changes light/standard/explore; `--housekeeper` explicitly changes compaction/title/summary. Client bootstrap also installs `opencode-cloud`, `opencode-local`, and `opencode-super` profiles. Easiest of all: just run `ferry opencode` on the client to write the opencode block below automatically. Every generated config also carries a fleet-identity `headers` map under `options` — `X-Ferry-Client` (this machine's name) and `X-Ferry-Fleet` (from `$FERRY_FLEET`, for a one-shot pin) — which `ferry opencode` / `ferry claude` write for you; see the `options` block below for the shape. Since fleets (2026-09-04) the host may run several complete routing sets behind these same bare lane names at once; which one you get depends on 'X-Ferry-Fleet', your sticky selection, or the host default — see README.md's Fleets section.

options.apiKey: <your device key (api_key in ~/.config/ferry/client.json), the master key, or "local" on a keyless LAN>

light.description: Worker for tasks rated 0-50 of 100 complexity: exploration follow-ups, small fixes, easy implementation, mechanical edits with clear instructions. Full tool access. Default worker; use standard only when the task clearly needs deeper judgment.

standard.description: Worker for tasks rated 51-100 of 100 complexity: multi-file implementation, ambiguous debugging, design judgment. Full tool access. Use light for anything rated 50 or below.

opencode._tip: Or just run `ferry opencode` on the client to write this automatically.

models.title: Ferry (heavy)
models.apiKey: <your device key (api_key in ~/.config/ferry/client.json), the master key, or "local" on a keyless LAN>
models._note: The domestic template serves six lanes at once: heavy + medium + flash + super-flash (cloud) and local-orch + local-sub (host GPU). Select medium explicitly for substantive coding or review work.

cline_vscode._warning: Close VS Code before writing these files: the Cline extension caches its config in memory and can overwrite your edits when it exits. Easiest of all: run `ferry cline` on the client — it writes exactly this, snapshots first.
_notes: chmod 600 ~/.cline/data/secrets.json — it holds the key in plain JSON.
The key must be non-empty even on a keyless LAN: Cline only sends an Authorization header when a key exists.
actModeApiProvider must be written as "openai" — a fresh install defaults it to "openrouter", and then Cline silently ignores providers.json entirely.
The provider id duality is Cline's own: extension state spells it "openai" (meaning OpenAI-Compatible), providers.json spells it "openai-compatible". Both files are required.

To pin a fleet, add "X-Ferry-Fleet": "<fleet>" to openAiHeaders and to the providers.json headers — a static file can't read $FERRY_FLEET, so the value is baked in by hand (or by `ferry cline` when the variable is set).
Merge into existing files: keep every key Cline already wrote that isn't shown here.

codex_cli._warning: Easiest of all: run `ferry codex` on the client — it installs exactly this as shell wrappers. Never edit ~/.codex/config.toml for this and never set CODEX_HOME: the wrappers pass everything as -c overrides so your ChatGPT login, history and config stay untouched.
codex_cli.by_hand: FERRY_CODEX_KEY=<LITELLM_MASTER_KEY or "local" on a keyless LAN> codex -c model_provider=ferry -c 'model_providers.ferry.name="Ferry"' -c 'model_providers.ferry.base_url="http://your-mac.local:8090/v1"' -c 'model_providers.ferry.env_key="FERRY_CODEX_KEY"' -c 'model_providers.ferry.wire_api="responses"' -c 'model_providers.ferry.http_headers={"X-Ferry-Client"="your-laptop"}' -c 'model="heavy"'
_notes: Codex 0.158+ only speaks the Responses API (wire_api = "responses"; "chat" is removed and config load fails on it), so the lane must serve /v1/responses.
base_url carries /v1 because Codex appends /responses itself.
The key travels in the FERRY_CODEX_KEY env var (env_key), never on argv.
Codex's /goal works through the wrappers. An unknown lane name only prints a non-fatal 'Model metadata not found' warning.

prime_agent._warning: Easiest of all: run `ferry prime` on the client — it edits models.json surgically (other providers and comments kept) and snapshots first. Not yet end-to-end tested against a live prime-agent.
_notes: The file is {"providers": {...}} (wrapped) and is JSONC: comments and trailing commas are fine.
baseUrl is the /v1 root: Prime Agent appends /chat/completions itself.
compat pins the plain OpenAI dialect (no store, no developer role, max_tokens) so a LiteLLM-fronted local lane accepts the request.
Merge into the existing file: keep every provider already there.

generic_openai_sdk_python.code:
from openai import OpenAI

client = OpenAI(
    base_url='http://your-mac.local:8090/v1',
    api_key='local'
)

response = client.chat.completions.create(
    model='heavy',
    messages=[{'role': 'user', 'content': 'Tell me a joke.'}]
)
print(response.choices[0].message.content)
